name: Dana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead at Harvest and Hearth, an upmarket supermarket in the nice end of town, where people buy sourdough, good cheese and wine. I run the deli and cheese counter with a team of four and cover the tills at peak times. I start at seven, set up the counter, check the stock and the use-by dates and then spend the day cutting, wrapping and talking about cheese.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I love is that people ask me for advice, like which cheese goes with a particular wine or how to feed twelve for Christmas. I'm good at it and I take pride in it. What wears me out is the Saturday crowds and the cold of the cheese room. I use AI every day. It helps me write the weekly special notices, plan the deli order, and it gave me a pricing sheet for my side business, which is a small home bakery that sells jam tarts and Polish poppyseed rolls on weekends. My fiancé Tomasz is a carpenter and we have a strong cushion, about a year, with plans for a wedding in the spring and a house after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world carries on and that's fine. At work I'd tell the team to keep using the tools we have, like the ordering helper. At church I'd say thank goodness, I need a calm year because we've got a wedding to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm fine and my plans stay. My job is about people, taste and trust, and my customers pay for the human. Tomasz has more work than he can do, so money isn't the issue. If anything bothers me it's prices, since the shop's costs keep climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, run the wedding in spring and start saving for the house, about eight hundred a month between us. I'd grow the home bakery, perhaps a market stall once a month. I'd keep using AI for planning and pricing, and I'd train the new girl on the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, honestly, it's a good moment in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the home bakery doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes about three hundred a month now, mostly from Sundays and a few orders from the church. The poppyseed rolls sell out, my grandmother's recipe. I'd like it to double by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think of the bakery as a backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, and also as something I enjoy. I'm not frightened of losing my job, but I like having something that's mine. It's good to have two legs.

say: I'd tell the team to keep using the **tools** we have, like the ordering helper.
I'd tell my church friends I need a **calm** year for the wedding.
think: My job is about taste and trust, so customers pay for the **human**.
Rising shop **costs** bother me more than AI.
do: Run the **wedding** in spring and save eight hundred a month for a house.
Grow the home **bakery**, perhaps with a monthly market stall.
Keep using **AI** for planning and pricing.
feel: **Calm** and happy, in a good moment in my life.
S0.quote: My job is about people, taste and trust, and my customers pay for the human.
fieldNote: Calm **matches** a secure job, a year's savings and a partner with plenty of work.
The bakery is both a hobby and a second leg, and she says so **plainly**.

steps.text: Keep running the deli counter and train the new girl
Save eight hundred a month towards a house
Double the home bakery with a monthly market stall
Keep using AI for ordering and pricing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a time to be sensible and to be kind to those who struggle. At work I'd say let's learn the tools and see where they help us. At church I'd say look after your neighbours, and I'd do a poppyseed roll collection for the food bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means more tools and fewer office jobs. Head office will use AI for ordering, planning, pricing and emails. My own job is the human end, advising and cutting, so I think it's fine, but they might ask me to run the counter with fewer people. I'd be okay with that if the pay matched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person at Harvest and Hearth who knows the AI ordering system best. I'd ask for the assistant manager spot, and I'd grow the home bakery to six hundred a month. Tomasz and I would carry on with the wedding and the house plans, and I'd teach the older staff to use the tools on my breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, calm. Maybe a little worried for the people who aren't using the tools yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which people are you worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barbara in the bakery section, who's fifty-six and refuses to touch the tablet. And Lukas, who's nineteen, thinks the tools do everything and doesn't check. I'd coach both, but in different ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you cope if head office cut counter staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good deli person is hard to replace, because customers buy more when there's someone to talk to. I'd show them the numbers, and I'd also be ready to move to a smaller premium shop.

say: I'd say be **sensible** and kind to those who struggle.
I'd run a roll **collection** for the food bank at church.
think: Head office will use AI for ordering, **planning**, pricing and emails.
My job is the human end, so I think I'm **fine**.
do: Become the **ordering** system expert at Harvest and Hearth.
Ask for **assistant manager** and grow the bakery to six hundred a month.
Teach older staff the **tools** on my breaks.
feel: **Calm**, with a little worry for people who haven't started on the tools.
S1.quote: A good deli person is hard to replace, because customers buy more when there's someone to talk to.
fieldNote: She stays calm **because** her job is the human end of a premium shop, and she already uses the tools.
She names **Barbara** and Lukas, and would coach each differently.

steps.text: Become the ordering system expert at Harvest and Hearth
Apply for assistant manager
Grow the bakery to six hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is cruel, it's too short for families to prepare. At work I'd say let's pull together and share what we know. At church I'd ask the priest to organise help for people who'd be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one that scares me. Thinking AI by 2028 hits office jobs everywhere, then robots around 2031 make a deli counter and till team much smaller. Premium customers might still want a human for a while, but the owners wouldn't pay for that if a robot was cheaper. Tomasz's carpentry is safer, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the bakery into a proper business, with a licence, a market stall and a website, so there's income if the shop cuts me. I'd keep the wedding but small, and put money into savings aiming for eighteen months of costs. I'd train as a chef or pastry cook, because food made by hands might last. And I'd look at a smaller shop that depends on service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. But I'm used to moving fast, and I'd push through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI every day in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because the people who use it well do better. It would write my business plan, handle my orders and check my sums. I'd just make sure the baking and the customers are still mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's make a plan with numbers on one page. He's not a talker, so I'd make it concrete, what we save, what we cut, what we'd do if one of us lost the job. He'd say okay, and mean it.

say: I'd say two years is **cruel**, too short for families to prepare.
I'd ask the priest at church to organise **help** for people left behind.
think: Robots around **2031** make a deli and till team much smaller.
Tomasz's carpentry is **safer**, but not forever.
do: Build the **bakery** into a licensed business with a stall and a website.
Keep a small **wedding** and aim for eighteen months of savings.
Train as a **pastry cook**, since food made by hand may last.
feel: **Anxious**, but used to moving fast and pushing through it.
S2.quote: Premium customers might still want a human for a while, but the owners wouldn't pay for that if a robot was cheaper.
fieldNote: She is **anxious** because the shop's owners would swap people for robots once cheaper, yet she acts at once.
Her **household** has a strong cushion and a hands-on partner, which keeps her short of alarmed.

steps.text: Get a licence and build a website for the home bakery
Save towards eighteen months of costs
Train as a pastry cook on evenings
Keep the wedding small to protect savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now, and I'd say that at work and at church. I'd tell the team to learn the tools and look after their money. I'd keep sharing my own experience with the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel good about five years. The thinking AI by 2031, the robots by 2034, and by then I'd have a proper business of my own and a family. I'd see it coming and be ready, which is what I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bakery in the first year to a small shop stall, and keep my job at Harvest and Hearth while it grows. I'd marry Tomasz in spring, buy a house within three years and have a baby after. I'd use AI for the paperwork and the planning, so I can spend my time baking and selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Five years is exactly the length of time I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shop stall look like in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A weekend stall at the town market, a trestle table with rolls, tarts and jam jars. About a hundred and fifty pounds of ingredients a week, and a profit of eight hundred a month by the end of the year. I'd have Tomasz build me a proper wooden display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give up the deli job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. Maybe in the fourth or fifth year, when the bakery pays well enough. I like the cheese counter, and the pay is good. I'd leave the cheese counter on my own terms, not because I'm pushed out by a robot.

I'd tell the team to learn the tools and look after their **money**.
think: By 2034 I'd have my own **business** and a family.
I'd see it coming and be **ready**, which is what I like.

feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, because five years is the length of time I'd want.
S3.quote: I'd leave the cheese counter on my own terms, not because I'm pushed out by a robot.
fieldNote: Five years suits an **adaptive** planner: she builds a business while holding the job and expects to leave by choice.
Her calm is based on money, a clear plan and a **partner** with steady trade work.

steps.text: Open a weekend market stall for the bakery within a year
Keep the deli job while the bakery grows
Marry Tomasz in spring and buy a house in three years
Use AI for paperwork and ordering at the stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing and I'd say it at church too. At work I'd tell the young staff that this is time to build a skill that lasts. I'd probably also post about the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel good. Ten years takes me to thirty-seven, with a family, a house and a bakery shop of my own. The robots at 2039 would be coming just as I'm established. I'd still keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Harvest and Hearth for a few years, then move to the bakery full time. I'd have the wedding, buy a house, have two children and keep saving about a thousand a month. I'd use the AI tools for everything that's not baking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and content. It's a long road, but I'm comfortable on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own bakery shop sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Polish and English bakes, bread, rolls, poppyseed cake and a few jam tarts, sold from a small shop with a window. Tomasz would build the shelves and the counter. We'd do corporate orders and weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if AI in ten years could bake and sell better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will pay for a bakery with a story and a grandmother's recipe, and if they don't, I'll do something else. I've always found something.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing**, and I'd say so at church.
I'd tell the young staff to build a **skill** that lasts.
think: By thirty-seven I'd have a family, a **house** and a bakery shop.
The robots in 2039 would arrive just as I'm **established**.
do: Stay at Harvest and Hearth a few years, then go **full time** at the bakery.
Marry, buy a house and have two **children**, saving a thousand a month.
Use AI for everything that isn't **baking**.
feel: **Calm** and content, comfortable on a long road.
S4.quote: People will pay for a bakery with a story and a grandmother's recipe, and if they don't, I'll do something else.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her turn a side **business** into a shop, so calm is the honest answer.
She says she'd find **something** else if the bakery failed, which fits her adaptive history.

steps.text: Move to the bakery full time after a few years at Harvest and Hearth
Save a thousand a month for the house and shop
Marry Tomasz, buy a house and have two children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Families would have no time to plan, and shops would rush. What would help is a clear plan from the government and employers, support for small businesses like my bakery, and training for the people who aren't already using these tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People think shop work is the end of the road, but mine has taught me to talk to anyone, price things and keep going. It also taught me to plan. I'd like people to see that those are real skills and that people like me can use them.

headlineQuote: People think shop work is the end of the road, but mine has taught me to talk to anyone, price things and keep going.
portrait: **Dana** is a 27-year-old team lead on the deli and cheese counter at Harvest and Hearth, an upmarket supermarket.
She is traditional and **adaptive**, uses AI every day and runs a small home bakery on weekends.
She is engaged to Tomasz, a **carpenter**, and has about a year of costs saved.
She is calm in most worlds, **anxious** if AGI is two years off, and always builds her own business.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because families and shops would have no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **plan** from government and employers, support for small businesses and training for people not yet using the tools.
